blogs.title: What If Biological Viruses Became Computer Viruses?
blogs.brief: Exploring the convergence of biology and cybersecurity: Could biological viruses ever become computer malware, and what happens when the line between data and organism blurs?
blogs.content:
![Computer Virus vs Biological Virus](https://img.magnific.com/premium-vector/computer-virus-design-vector-illustration-eps10-graphic_1120563-32254.jpg?semt=ais_hybrid&w=740&q=80)

With the title **"What If Biological Viruses Became Computer Viruses?"**, a number of questions arise: Could such a virus become an unstoppable form of malicious code? How would computer systems respond to it, and what would it mean for the future of technology? Could an attack of this nature bring modern computing to an end?

Cybersecurity often takes inspiration from nature. Defenders seek to emulate the human immune system when they hunt down the cyber equivalents of biological viruses, bacterial infections, and parasites.

We are dealing with two very different hosts one a biological organism formed by millions of years of evolution, the other involving computer systems coded by humans over decades. Biological viruses can cause suffering and even death, and while cyberattacks may cause indirect suffering to people if made on health systems, their impact is mostly loss of business, money, data, and reputation.

The analogy between computer security problems and biological processes was recognized as early as 1987, when the term *computer virus* was introduced by [Leonard Adelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Adleman). Later, [Gene Spafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Spafford) argued that computer viruses are a form of artificial life.

# Biological Viruses Vs Computer Viruses

## What is a Biological Virus?

A [biological virus](https://www.biologyonline.com/tutorials/biological-viruses) is a tiny invader that cannot survive on its own; it needs a living cell to multiply. Once inside, it hijacks the cell's system to create more viruses, often making you sick in the process.

It spreads through touch, air, fluids, or even insects like mosquitoes. Think of viruses like COVID-19, flu, or HIV they are fast, sneaky, and hard to stop without vaccines or strong immunity. One infected person or surface can spark a chain reaction.

## What is a Computer Virus?

A [computer virus](https://documents.uow.edu.au/~jennie/WEBPDF/1997_09.pdf) is malicious code that hides in files and spreads when opened. It can corrupt data, slow systems, or steal information, often triggered by a simple click. Like a digital parasite, it thrives on unprotected devices.

Most computer viruses rely on user interaction, such as clicking a malicious link, downloading an infected file, or using an unprotected USB drive.

> Biological and computer viruses may appear differently under a microscope or on a dashboard, but both share the same mission: to invade, spread, and disrupt.

# What If Virus DNA/RNA Turns into Malicious Computer Code?

Biological viruses are unpredictable because they evolve when interacting with living organisms and changing environments. On the other hand, computer viruses are predictable because they are programmed to exploit specific systems evolving only through a programmer's touch.

If we compare them, *"A Denial of Service (DoS) attack can be compared to HIV (Human immunodeficiency virus), because both aim at overloading a system,"* said Ruchna Nigam, security researcher at Fortinet.

However, human and computer viruses could converge in the future. Most human viruses are essentially DNA or RNA code strands containing essential genetic instructions for living organisms. *A biological virus is information that codes for behavior in a host system.* It is theoretically possible to craft synthetic DNA sequences that, once transcribed into digital bits by DNA sequencers, exploit software vulnerabilities in processing software.

Researchers from the University of Washington demonstrated this concept by injecting malware directly into DNA strands:

<iframe width="100%" height="400" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/F9HScPlBFhM" title="Researchers inject malicious code into DNA strands" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" allowfullscreen></iframe>

*"When this physical DNA strand was sequenced and processed by the vulnerable program, it gave remote control of the computer doing the processing. That is, we were able to remotely exploit and gain full control over a computer using adversarial synthetic DNA."

The researchers encoded malware using the four bases in DNA Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G), and Thymine (T). When read by DNA sequencing equipment, the molecular code converted into executable computer code capable of taking over the connected machine.

While this hack relied on a specific flaw in DNA sequencing software under controlled lab conditions, it proved that the boundary between physical biological data and digital code can be crossed.

# What If COVID-19 Were a Computer Virus?

Imagine, as a hypothetical scenario, that a COVID-19-like computer virus emerged within a major IT Company from Wuhan, China. Rather than requiring a user to click a link or download an infected file, the malware could spread across internet-connected devices like an biological virus spreads between human hosts.

In this scenario, the virus could infect multiple operating systems and critical infrastructure, potentially disrupting hospitals, power grids, financial systems, and essential public services that makes the mankind return to stone-age. Over several years, millions of devices could be compromised, causing severe social and economic consequences.

This thought experiment highlights how a self-propagating worm capable of spreading without conventional user interaction could challenge the computer security and resilience of global computing networks.

# Conclusion

Biological viruses and computer viruses are not identical, but they share one fundamental trait: neither can function without a host. A biological virus is the product of millions of years of evolution, whereas a computer virus is engineered by human code.

Can a biological virus "become" malware in the wild? Not with current technology. However, researchers have demonstrated that molecular DNA data can trigger vulnerabilities in hardware and sequencing software under specific laboratory conditions.

Would such threats spell doom for modern computing? Unlikely—security systems continuously evolve to counter novel vectors. What is certain, however, is that cybersecurity will increasingly expand into unconventional domains wherever physical and biological data transition into digital bits.

> **Sources & References:**
> - [Computer Immunology (ACM Digital Library)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/262793.262811)
> - [Human Virology & Malware (Fortinet Research)](https://media.blackhat.com/bh-eu-12/Lovet/bh-eu-12-Lovet-Human_Virology-WP.pdf)
> - [Antivirus & Biological Frontier (CIO)](https://www.cio.com/article/284357/antivirus-software-computer-viruses-could-cross-frontier-into-biological-realm-researchers-say.html)
> - [Malicious Code Written into DNA (TechCrunch)](https://techcrunch.com/2017/08/09/malicious-code-written-into-dna-infects-the-computer-that-reads-it/)

blogs.title: Building an Android-Based Home Server with Termux, Jellyfin, and Samba
blogs.brief: Learn how to transform your smartphone into a functional LAN-based media streaming and file-sharing server using Termux, Jellyfin, and Samba.
blogs.content:
# Building an Android-Based Home Server with Termux, Jellyfin, and Samba

## Introduction

Home servers are traditionally built on dedicated machines such as old desktops, NAS devices, or single-board computers. However, modern smartphones are powerful enough to handle lightweight server workloads. This project demonstrates how an Android device can be transformed into a functional home server using Termux.

The objective was to build a LAN-based media and file server using:

* Jellyfin for media streaming
* Samba for file sharing
* SSH for remote access and management

---

## Why Use Android as a Home Server?

Using Android provides:

* Low power consumption
* No additional hardware cost
* Portability
* Sufficient performance for personal use

Limitations:

* No root access
* Background process restrictions
* Networking constraints

With proper configuration, these limitations can be managed.
My Spec Sheet for My Android is 256GB Storage, With 8GB RAM.

---

## Step 1: Installing and Setting Up Termux

Termux provides a Linux-like environment on Android.

### Installation

Install Termux from F-Droid (recommended).

### Initial Setup

```bash
pkg update && pkg upgrade -y
pkg install git curl wget nano -y
```

### Enable Storage Access

```bash
termux-setup-storage
```

---

## Step 2: Prevent Android from Killing the Server

Android aggressively kills background apps, which can stop your server.

### Enable Developer Options

* Go to Settings -> About Phone
* Tap Build Number 7 times

### Configure Developer Settings

* Ensure "Don't keep activities" is OFF
* Set Background process limit -> Standard limit

### Disable Battery Optimization

* Settings -> Apps -> Termux -> Battery
* Set to Unrestricted / No restrictions

Optional:

* Lock Termux in recent apps
* Disable system cleaner apps

This step is critical for stability.

---

## Step 3: Installing Required Packages

Install core components:

```bash
pkg install openssh samba ffmpeg wget tar -y
```

* OpenSSH (Remote Access)
* Samba (file sharing)
* FFmpeg (required by Jellyfin)

---

## Step 4: Setting Up SSH

SSH allows remote access and file transfer.

```bash
sshd -p 2222
passwd
```

Access from another device:

```bash
ssh user@192.168.x.x -p 2222
```

---

## Step 5: Installing Jellyfin

Jellyfin is not available directly via Termux packages, so it must be installed manually.

### Download Jellyfin

```bash
wget https://repo.jellyfin.org/releases/server/linux/stable/latest/jellyfin-server-linux-arm64.tar.gz
```

### Extract and Setup

```bash
tar -xvf jellyfin-server-linux-arm64.tar.gz
mv jellyfin_* jellyfin
cd jellyfin
```

### Run Jellyfin

```bash
./jellyfin
```

### Create Media Directory

```bash
mkdir -p ~/media/{movies,tv,music}
```

### Configure Samba

```bash
nano $PREFIX/etc/samba/smb.conf
```

```ini
[global]
   workgroup = WORKGROUP
   server string = Termux Server
   security = user
   map to guest = Bad User
   smb ports = 4455

[media]
   path = /data/data/com.termux/files/home/media
   browseable = yes
   writable = yes
   guest ok = yes
```

### Start Samba

```bash
smbd -s $PREFIX/etc/samba/smb.conf
```

---

## Step 6: Configuring Jellyfin

Open a browser on the same network:

```
http://<PHONE_IP>:8096
```

### Initial Setup

1. Create admin account
2. Select language
3. Add media libraries

### Media Paths

* Movies → `/data/data/com.termux/files/home/media/movies`
* TV → `/data/data/com.termux/files/home/media/tv`
* Music → `/data/data/com.termux/files/home/media/music`

### Recommended Structure

```
media/
├── movies/
├── tv/
└── music/
```

Jellyfin scans these directories and fetches metadata automatically.

---

## Step 7: Setting Up Samba

### Create Media Directory

```bash
mkdir -p ~/media/{movies,tv,music}
```

### Configure Samba

```bash
nano $PREFIX/etc/samba/smb.conf
```

```ini
[global]
   workgroup = WORKGROUP
   server string = Termux Server
   security = user
   map to guest = Bad User
   smb ports = 4455

[media]
   path = /data/data/com.termux/files/home/media
   browseable = yes
   writable = yes
   guest ok = yes
```

### Start Samba

```bash
smbd -s $PREFIX/etc/samba/smb.conf
```

---

## Step 8: Accessing the Server on LAN

### Find IP Address

```bash
ip route
```

Example:

```
192.168.100.73
```

---

### Access Methods

## Jellyfin (Media Streaming)

```
http://192.168.100.73:8096
```

## Samba (File Sharing)

Windows:

```
\\192.168.100.73:4455\media
```

Linux:

```bash
smbclient //192.168.100.73/media -p 4455 -N
```

### SSH / SFTP

```bash
sftp -P 2222 user@192.168.100.73
```

---

## Step 9: Automation

Edit `.bashrc`:

```bash
nano ~/.bashrc
```

Add:

```bash
# Start SSH
if ! pgrep sshd >/dev/null; then
    sshd -p 2222 &
fi

# Start Samba
if ! pgrep smbd >/dev/null; then
    smbd -s $PREFIX/etc/samba/smb.conf &
fi

# Start Jellyfin
if ! pgrep -f jellyfin >/dev/null; then
    ~/jellyfin/jellyfin >/dev/null 2>&1 &
fi
```

---

## Challenges and Limitations

* Android may kill background processes
* Samba uses non-standard ports
* Limited performance compared to dedicated servers
* Not suitable for public exposure

---

## Conclusion

Transforming an Android device into a home server with Termux demonstrates how far lightweight, software-defined infrastructure can go. By combining Jellyfin for media streaming, Samba for file sharing, and SSH for management, we built a system that follows traditional server design principles while running on unconventional hardware.
The real challenge in this setup is not installation, but stability specifically working around Android’s aggressive process management. Once background restrictions are properly configured, the system becomes reliable enough for consistent LAN use.
While this setup is not a replacement for a dedicated Linux server, it serves as a highly efficient and cost-effective solution for personal use. It is especially useful for learning, experimentation, and small-scale media hosting.
### Future Improvements

Right Now  The Server is Only Accessible on LAN, But I am Planning to Make it Accessible on the Internet, Stay Tuned for that!
